units.translation: 277-78a. Aea at least even now remains: He says that Aea has remained unbroken from the time of Sesonchosis until his own day, and that those descendants are of the people settled by Sesonchosis. For he has called these 'grandsons' loosely, just as Heracleidae are called not only the children of Heracles, but also their descendants. Thus also those in Scythia are descendants of the Egyptians, as Apollonius too says. And Scymnus says in his work on Asia that the Colchians are colonists of the Egyptians. And Herodorus in Book 2 (104 sq.) mentions the circumcision of their private parts and the weaving of linen, and says that they use the customs of the Egyptians.

279-81a. They indeed with painted tablets: There are, he says, among them also laws of their ancestors and pillars, on which are inscribed records of land and sea.

b. kyrbeis: pillars. He means the axones, on which the laws are written, as the comic poet Aristophanes (Birds 1354). But Apollodorus (244 F 107b J.) says that every public writing and laws are called a kyrbis, because the ancients, setting up stones, inscribed what had been decided, calling them stelae from their standing, and kyrbeis from their rising to a height because of being topped off, as it were kyrpheis. Later, writing on whitened wooden tablets, they called them the same. A kyrbis, then, is that which contains the sacred records.
